turns.text: Hi, I'm Marco. I'm here for the frontend engineer screening. Ready when you are.

Hi Marco, nice to meet you. Thanks for joining the frontend engineer screening. There are three questions, and I'll ask them one at a time. Take as long as you need on each.

**Question 1:** What causes a React component to re-render?

tool_events.name: get_question
tool_events.output: {"id": "q1", "text": "What causes a React component to re-render?", "rubric": "state/props/context change, parent re-render, new references"}

turns.text: Sure. A component re-renders when its state changes via setState or a useState setter, when its parent re-renders (by default children re-render even if props are the same, unless you wrap them in React.memo), or when a context it consumes via useContext gets a new value. Also custom hooks that use state or context internally will trigger it. Worth noting that a re-render doesn't necessarily mean a DOM update, React diffs the output and only commits what changed. If you want to avoid unnecessary ones you'd use memo, useMemo/useCallback for stable references, or split context so consumers only subscribe to what they need.

Thanks, that's clear.

**Question 2:** Explain the JavaScript event loop in about a minute.

tool_events.name: get_question
tool_events.output: {"id": "q2", "text": "Explain the event loop in one minute.", "rubric": "call stack, task queue, microtasks"}

turns.text: Ok. JS runs on a single thread with a call stack. Synchronous code runs to completion first. When you hit async stuff like setTimeout, fetch, DOM events, the browser (or Node) handles them outside the stack and queues callbacks when they're ready. The event loop checks: if the call stack is empty, it first drains the entire microtask queue, which is promise callbacks, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver, and then takes one task from the macrotask queue, like a setTimeout or an event handler, runs it, drains microtasks again, and so on. In the browser, rendering typically happens between tasks, which is why a long sync loop or an endless microtask chain blocks paint. Classic example: console.log 1, setTimeout log 2, Promise.resolve().then log 3, log 4 gives you 1, 4, 3, 2.

Nice, and the example helps.

**Question 3, the last one:** How do you avoid layout thrashing?

tool_events.name: get_question
tool_events.output: {"id": "q3", "text": "How do you avoid layout thrashing?", "rubric": "batch reads/writes, requestAnimationFrame"}

turns.text: Layout thrashing is when you interleave DOM reads and writes in a loop, like reading offsetHeight, then setting a style, then reading again, which forces the browser to do synchronous layout over and over. The fix is mainly batching: do all your reads first, then all your writes. requestAnimationFrame helps to schedule writes right before the next frame, and libraries like fastdom formalize the read/write split. Beyond that, cache measurements instead of re-querying, prefer transform and opacity for animations since they skip layout and can go to the compositor, use ResizeObserver or IntersectionObserver instead of polling geometry, and toggle a class instead of setting lots of individual styles. CSS containment (contain: layout) can also limit how much of the page gets recalculated. The Performance panel in DevTools will flag forced reflows if you want to confirm.
Thanks, Marco. That was the last question. You've finished the frontend screening, and I've sent in the report. The hiring team will review it and contact you about next steps. Good luck!
